Q: Can't install nuget package in VS 2022 A:

You should not explicitly include the package "Microsoft.NETCore.Platforms" in your project. This is a system support package and included automatically if you need it. Since its latest version is 8.0.0-preview-something, I belive it is no longer necessary at all for projects targetting .NET 8.0 or later. Just remove any reference to that package from your project.

Apparently things have changed and there is something called "Auto MDI-X" on Gigabit ethernet ports, so you shouldn't need a crossover cable, but maybe check the ports to make sure that they both support that.

Q: Property spring.cloud.config.import-check.enabled removed A:

In the newer spring cloud versions you should use spring.config.import instead of depending on spring.cloud.config.import-check.enabled

For an optional config server: spring.config.import=optional:configserver:

or with URL: spring.cloud.import=optional:configserver:http://localhost:8888

This is the approach documented by Spring Cloud Config: https://docs.spring.io/spring-cloud-config/reference/client.html

For tests where Config Server should not be used, put this in the test properteis/profie:

spring.config.import=
spring.cloud.config.enabled=false

The error is happening because Config Client is on the classpath and Spring Cloud expects a 'configserver:' import unless you explicitly make it optional or disable it for that environment.

Q: How to handle class imbalance in PyTorch when using ImageFolder for medical image classification? A:

Your dataset has a massive flaw: the "disease" (Pneumonia) is the majority of the data. That almost never happens in the real world. My project will teach you a more advanced way of tackling these. In our FDA project, we are dealing with a realistic pattern: 98% of clinical trials are perfectly fine ("Active"). Only a tiny, rare 2% end in disaster ("Halted"). A smoke detector spends 99.9% of its life doing nothing, ignoring the clean air (the 98% Active trials). But the second it senses smoke (the 2% Halt), it screams. We are building the mathematical "smoke detector" for pharmaceutical companies.This will force us to use Focal Loss to handle extreme data imbalance.  But we will use both BCE + Focal Loss.

mild_thresh

  • What it is: A threshold value that defines “mild imbalance”. It’s a number between 0 and 1 (typically something like 0.10 or 10%).

Prevalence_ratio(halt_fraction)

which is the universal medical/statistical term for "how often the rare thing happens".

  • What it is: The fraction of my dataset that belongs to the minority class (the one I am most interested in catching in this project).

  • In my project: The minority class is halted (label 0).
    If out of 100 time steps, 5 are halted, then prevalence_ratio = 5 / 100 = 0.05 (5%).

  • The smaller the number, the more extreme the imbalance, and the more we need to focus the model on the rare halts.

If halt fraction ≥ 10% → plain BCE. The data is balanced enough.

If 1% ≤ halt fraction < 10% → weighted BCE. This gently pushes the model to care about the minority class.

If halt fraction < 1% → Focal Loss. Extreme rarity demands focal loss mechanism. It forces the model to focus on hard, misclassified samples (the halts). A teacher who doesn’t care about the easy questions . But only cares if the student can solve the toughest questions(fewer in number) or not.

Focal Loss does two things:

  1. It turns down the volume on the easy "active" samples (like weighted BCE does).

  2. It also zooms in on the hard mistakes – the halts the model is still confidently wrong about.

Alpha fixes the data distribution. Gamma fixes the model's overconfidence.

  • Alpha ensures the rare 1% is treated like it's 99%.

  • Gamma(usually 2.0) ensures the model ignores easy questions and obsesses over hard mistakes.

  • The Clamp (max/min) ensures the math doesn't hit zero and crash the server.

This is exactly how PyTorch’s C++ backend wires the alpha parameter:

  • It multiplies alpha against Class 1 (The noisy Actives).

  • It multiplies (1 - alpha) against Class 0 (The rare Halts).

The Flip for our project : If our Halts are at 0.5% (0.005), we set alpha equal to that tiny number.

  • Class 1 (Actives) gets a base weight of 0.005 (0.5%).

  • Class 0 (Halts) automatically gets 1.0 - 0.005 = 0.995 (99.5%).

If you are an audio engineer, and the drums (Class 1) are beating so loud that you are not able to hear the song from the singer (Class 0), but your soundboard only has a volume knob for the drums, what do you do? You turn the drums down. We want active to be almost silent, so alpha should be tiny – for example, if halts are 2% of the data, we’d set alpha = 0.02.

  • pos_weight = 1.0: The drums are at 100% volume.

  • pos_weight = 0.02: You just turned the drums down to 2% volume. They are now whispering.

Because the drums are whispering, the singer (who stayed exactly the same) suddenly sounds perfectly clear.  This is what we will do exactly.

If pos_weight = 1.0, both classes contribute equally.

If pos_weight > 1.0, the model is penalized more for misclassifying positive examples. If pos_weight < 1.0, the positive class is down-weighted. This is exactly what we need, because our positive class (active) is the majority, and we want to reduce its influence.

Then, pos_weight = number of positive samples / number of negative samples​= N0 /  N1

We want a value < 1 because we want to down-weight the majority (positive) class.We will set pos_weight < 1 to shrink the gradient contribution of the majority (active) class, so that the minority (halted) class gets a fair share of the model’s attention.  So the actual formula we used is:

In our project:

  • N0​ = number of halted samples (label = 0).

  • N1​ = number of active samples (label = 1).​

N0 / N1 = halt_ratio / (1− halt_ratio)

This is what we will use.

weight_val = safe_ratio / (1.0 - safe_ratio) ​​

Dividing them gives: halt_fraction ÷ active fraction.

The Goal: The total loss from all Active samples =  The total loss from all Halted samples.

  • safe_ratio is the percentage of FDA Halts (e.g., 0.05, or 5%).

  • (1.0 - safe_ratio) is the percentage of Active trials (e.g., 0.95, or 95%).

If you have 5 Halts and 95 Active trials, you divide them: 0.05/0.95=0.052.

This number (0.052) is your new volume setting. You are telling the system: " The Active trials are too loud. Shrink their gradient penalty down to 5.2% of its normal strength*."*

The Code could be something like below :

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision.ops import sigmoid_focal_loss


class ClinicalFocalLoss(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, prevalence_ratio, mild_thresh : float = 0.2, 
                extreme_thresh: float = 0.05, focal_thresh: float = 2.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.alpha = max(0.01, min(0.99, prevalence_ratio))
        # Balanced. gamma = 0 mathametically collapses into standard BCE
        if prevalence_ratio >= mild_thresh:
            self.gamma = 0.00
            
        elif prevalence_ratio >= extreme_thresh:
            # Mild Imbalance :  gamma = 0 + alpha creates Weighted BCE
            self.gamma = 0.00 
            
        else: 
            # Extreme imbalance = Full Focal suppression activated
            self.gamma = focal_gamma
            
    def forward(self):
        return sigmoid_focal_loss(
        logits,
        labels, 
        alpha = self.alpha, 
        gamma = self.gamma, 
        reduction = 'mean')

Q: Async Telegram bot freezes while processing voice messages with external API request A:

Your function post is not async. Convert it to async with such async tools like aiohttp or other instead requests

Q: Read only the first line of a file? A:

Use the .readline() method:

with open('myfile.txt') as f:
    first_line = f.readline()

Note that unless it is the only line in the file, the string returned from f.readline() will contain a trailing newline. You may wish to use

with open('myfile.txt') as f:
    first_line = f.readline().strip('\n')

instead, to remove the newline.

Q: ASP.NET Core Blazor Input Radio Group not binding A:

Because you have <html> tags inside your page, you are likely using the new .NET 8+ Blazor Web App template. By default, pages use Static Server-Side Rendering (Static SSR), meaning the page renders once and has no live connection to listen for clicks.

Adding an interactive render mode will hopefully fix your problem. Add this attribute directly below your @page "/" directive to enable live UI updates.

@attribute [RenderModeInteractiveServer]

note: Having <!doctype html>, <head>, and <body> tags inside an individual page component like Index.razor is generally bad practice. Those structural layout tags belong in your root App.razor file, while your pages should only contain the actual content and form elements.
